entities.name: Ravenna Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Ravenna Cathedral (Cattedrale dell'Assunzione di Maria Vergine) and the complex of Early Christian and Byzantine monuments surrounding it in Ravenna, Italy, represent the world's most complete surviving collection of early Byzantine mosaics, dating from the 5th and 6th centuries CE when Ravenna served as capital of the Western Roman Empire (402-476 CE), the Ostrogothic Kingdom (493-540 CE), and the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna (540-751 CE). The eight UNESCO-listed Ravenna monuments contain mosaics of extraordinary quality from every phase of this period.

Ravenna's mosaics span the three great political-religious phases: the Western Roman/Arian Christian period (Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Baptistery of Neon), the Ostrogothic/Arian period (Arian Baptistery, Theodoric's Palace), and the Byzantine/Orthodox period (San Vitale, Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Sant'Apollinare in Classe). San Vitale's famous mosaic panels showing Emperor Justinian I and Empress Theodora (c. 547 CE) are the finest surviving portraits of Byzantine imperial power.

Dante Alighieri, exiled from Florence in 1302, spent his final years in Ravenna (1318-1321), completing the Divine Comedy there and dying in the city. His tomb in Ravenna remains a pilgrimage site; Florence has periodically requested his remains but Ravenna refuses. Ravenna's combination of the world's greatest Byzantine mosaics and Dante's tomb makes it among Italy's most culturally significant cities beyond Rome and Florence.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ravenna's mosaic complex preserves more of the ancient and early medieval world in a single city than any other site in Western Europe — spanning Roman, Ostrogothic, and Byzantine civilization in continuous artistic program across 350 years.
